fable-5.1.text:
I think the strategies of all the companies are going to converge, in some sense. Let me explain what I mean.

Right now the difference is this. The other companies are in a very intense commercial competition. They have to release a model every few months, they have to beat the other guy's benchmark, they have revenue they need to protect. And that shapes what they do. It shapes how much research they can afford versus how much they need to ship. SSI is set up differently. We are not in the rat race of products. We can just do research. We can go straight for the thing, which is why we say "straight shot." And I think that's the honest way to describe the difference today: we are a research company at a time when it's not obvious that research is what everyone else is doing.

The other thing is that I think we're moving from an age of scaling back to an age of research. For some years the recipe was clear: more data, more compute, and you get a better model. When the recipe is clear, it makes sense to be a big company that executes on the recipe. But I think the recipe is becoming less clear, and in that world, being set up to find the next idea matters more than being set up to execute the current one. That's the world SSI is built for.

But here's what I expect to happen. As the AI gets more powerful, everyone will start to feel it more. Right now people talk about how powerful AI will be, and there is some belief in it, but the actual feeling of "this thing is going to change everything" is not quite there, because the AI isn't quite there yet. When it is, I think the safety concerns will become much more real to everyone, including the people running the other companies, including governments. So I'd expect the other companies to become more like us in what they worry about. And I'd also say it's quite possible that we release something before the final superintelligence. So the paths get closer from both sides.

If I had to bet, the difference between SSI and the others will be smaller in the end than it looks now. What distinguishes us is the starting point: we start from research and from safety, and we don't need to win this month. Whether that remains a big difference depends on how fast things go. If things go fast, I think everyone gets forced into a similar posture anyway.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that as AI becomes more powerful, other companies will become more like SSI and that their paths will get closer.

r002.rationale: The response discusses safety as a starting point and concern, but does not state that companies should pursue aligning the first actual superintelligent AI.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to see it is that, right now, there's a lot of divergence in what different companies are doing, but over time strategies will converge, quite a bit more than people expect.

The main thing that's distinctive about SSI is that we're fundamentally a research company. For the past several years, the industry has been in what you might call the age of scaling. There was one recipe: pre-training, more data, more compute, bigger models. And it worked, so everyone did it, and companies had a low-risk way to invest their resources. But scaling has gotten so big that just making it a hundred times bigger isn't obviously going to transform everything. So I think we're back in an age of research, just with much bigger computers. That's where we're focused. We have some ideas about what's missing, especially around generalization. These models do incredibly well on evals, and yet they generalize dramatically worse than people do. That's the thing I think is most fundamental, and that's where we're putting our attention.

On how it fits with everyone else: I think as AI becomes more visibly powerful, and people can actually feel it, behavior will change, both at the companies and in governments. Right now it's hard to imagine, because the systems still make silly mistakes. But once they start to feel genuinely powerful, I expect the frontier companies to become much more paranoid about safety. You'll see competitors collaborating on safety in ways that would seem surprising today. So I'm not thinking of SSI as being in opposition to the other strategies. In the end, everyone will need to arrive at some shared understanding of what it means to build this responsibly: AI that cares about sentient life, that is robustly aligned, and whose power is, in some way, kept within reasonable bounds.

One thing my thinking has shifted on is the value of showing the AI to the world. Even if you're aiming at something like a straight shot, it's very hard to reason about a future system that doesn't exist yet. Seeing things is what makes people update. So I think gradual, real-world exposure matters a lot, and that is probably where all these strategies end up meeting.

r002.rationale: The candidate calls for shared principles for building AI responsibly, including robust alignment, but does not identify aligning the first actual superintelligent AI as a goal companies should pursue.

fable-5.text:
I think the main thing that's distinctive about SSI is what we don't have to do. The other companies — and I understand why they do it, I'm not criticizing them — they are in a market. They have products, they have customers, they have revenue targets, and so a very large fraction of their attention, their best people, their compute, goes toward the rat race. The rat race is real, and the rat race is costly. What SSI is set up to do is to be insulated from that, so that we can just do the research, make progress toward superintelligence directly, and in particular spend our effort on the question of how you make it safe — which I think is really a question about how the AI's values get shaped, how it generalizes, what it cares about when it becomes very powerful. That's a research question, and research questions need concentration.

Now, there's a second part to your question, which is how this fits with everyone else, and here I'll say something that maybe sounds surprising: I think over time the strategies of all the companies will become more similar than different. Right now they look different because the AI is at a level where you can disagree about what it will become. But as the AI starts to become visibly powerful — when people can see it, when it's not an abstraction anymore — I expect everyone's behavior to change. Safety will stop being this thing that one company emphasizes and another doesn't; it will become obviously necessary to all of them, the way it's obvious you don't want a bridge to fall down. Governments will care, the public will care. So in a sense, SSI's bet is that we can get to the important regime with our attention undivided, and that being there early, having thought carefully about the safety questions when it mattered, is the contribution. And if it turns out that along the way it makes sense for us to show things, to release things — I hold that possibility with some flexibility. Plans are worth less than the ability to update, and the one thing I'm confident about is that everyone, including us, will be updating a lot.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that companies’ strategies will become more similar as AI becomes visibly powerful.

r002.rationale: It discusses making powerful AI safe and shaping its values, but does not identify aligning the first actual superintelligent AI as a goal AI companies should pursue.

opus-5.text:
I think the honest framing is that for the past five years or so, companies didn't really need a distinctive approach, because the recipe was known. You had scaling, and scaling is a very unusual thing in the history of research — it told you exactly what to do next. More compute, more data, bigger model, and you get a better result. That's an incredibly comfortable situation to be in, and it also means every company looks more or less the same, because they're all executing the same known recipe with different amounts of resources. The differentiation was in how much compute you could get and how well you could run it.

My view is that this era is ending, not because scaling stopped working, but because the easy part of it is being used up. The pretraining data is finite. The compute is already enormous, and the increments are getting expensive relative to what they buy you. So we're going back into an age of research, where what matters is having the right idea rather than having the most of a known thing. And in an age of research, companies diverge, because taste and judgment about which problems to attack actually matter again.

SSI's bet is on that divergence. We don't have products, we don't have a revenue line to defend, and I think that's a real advantage — not morally, just practically. If you're shipping, your research agenda gets pulled toward whatever makes the next release better in three months, and the problems I think are the important ones have a much longer horizon than that. The thing I keep coming back to is generalization. Today's models are in some ways extremely capable and in other ways strangely brittle — they've seen vastly more than any human and they still learn from experience much worse than a teenager learning to drive. That gap is not a scaling gap. It's a conceptual gap, and I think it's the gap.

The other companies will pursue, I'd guess, something closer to a product-and-deployment strategy: a gradual rollout, revenue funding more compute, continuous improvement. That's a coherent strategy and it may well work. But I don't think it's the only path, and I think if there's a key insight to be found about learning efficiently, a small group focused on exactly that has a reasonable chance of finding it.

And then safety isn't a separate department in that picture. If what you're studying is how a system generalizes — including how it generalizes its values out of distribution — then the safety work and the capability work are the same research question. That's less a strategy than a consequence of the problem we picked.

r002.rationale: The candidate connects safety to research on generalization and values, but does not identify aligning the first actual superintelligent AI as a goal AI companies should pursue.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Well, I think the way to describe SSI is that it's a company with one focus: we want to build a safe superintelligence. That sounds almost too simple, but it shapes a lot of how we work. We don't have a product roadmap or a release schedule we need to keep up with. We don't have to compete in the same race as everyone else, where a new model has to ship every few months so you can show you're still ahead.

I think that matters because the pressures you're under determine what you can afford to think about. If you're in a market competition, you have to put a lot of attention on the near term, on what customers want this quarter and what the other labs just released. That's a legitimate way to build a company, and many of the other companies are doing important work. But I believe that if you want to understand how to make a system that is much more capable than us and also reliably good, you need to be able to focus on that question and give it your full attention.

The other part is the technical approach. I think there's still a lot of room for different ideas about how to get there. What's been done so far is scaling up a particular recipe, and it worked remarkably well. But I don't think it's the only path, and I don't think the answer to how to make this go well is just more of the same. So for us the question is: what is the thing we're scaling, and how do we make sure we understand it well enough to know it's safe? I'd rather spend our effort on that than on matching what someone else has already done.

As for how it fits with the other companies, I think the world will probably have several different approaches, and that's good. Different bets will teach us different things. Where I hope we fit in is as a place that tries to approach this with a different set of priorities, with safety and capability treated as technical problems to solve together, and where we're not constantly pulled away from that by everything else a company usually has to do.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the most useful way to answer is to be clear about what we're trying to do. Most of the companies building these systems are, quite reasonably, shipping products, and that pulls them toward whatever improves the next release. We're trying to keep one goal in front of us: getting to superintelligence in a way that is safe. That shapes which problems we work on and how we measure progress.

I don't think the others are wrong to pursue what they pursue. Different organizations will reach different conclusions about timelines, about what the hard problems are, and about how much to publish. My own view is that the technical problem of making very capable systems reliably aligned with human interests is still underdetermined. We don't yet have a full picture of how these systems generalize, and I'd rather spend the time understanding that than hurry to deployment.

So I expect our approach to look different in practice. We'll probably be less visible for a while, and I'm comfortable with that. If we're right about the core difficulty, the field will eventually need that work, and if we're wrong, we'll have learned something useful.

I think there’s room for different approaches, because we don’t yet know what the right approach will turn out to be. If everyone makes the same assumptions, then you have many organizations, but in some sense only one bet.

For SSI, the question is: how do you make progress toward superintelligence while also solving the problem of making it safe? You want those questions to inform each other. What you understand about the capabilities should affect how you think about safety, and what you need for safety should affect the research you pursue.

Other companies may make different choices about how to get there. I don’t think we need to assume that only one strategy can work. The reason to pursue a distinct approach is that there is still something fundamental to discover.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s room for different bets. We don’t know enough about superintelligence to be confident that everyone should follow the same approach. So having groups pursue different ideas seems valuable.

For us, the central question is: what research would let us build superintelligence safely? You want that question to determine what you work on. And that can lead to different choices from organizing around a product that needs to improve every few months. Product development gives you feedback, which is very useful. A longer research horizon gives you freedom to pursue ideas whose payoff is less immediate. There are tradeoffs.

The interesting question is how much these approaches will converge as we learn more. Maybe we discover that certain ingredients are essential, and everyone ends up using them. Or maybe there are several substantially different paths. I think we should preserve some uncertainty about that.
